The evidence shows modest or poor accuracy, not that no calculator is ever useful.

question: Does the familial transmission of drinking patterns persist into young adulthood?
answer: The only directly relevant study (Swedish 10-year follow-up) found limited persistence: offspring of abstaining families drank substantially less in young adulthood, but actual drinking levels in drinking families were not or only weakly associated with offspring drinking. The other records do not address transmission into young adulthood.

claims.text: In a Swedish longitudinal study (n=744), young adults from families that were abstainers in 2000 drank substantially less in 2010 than offspring of non-abstaining families, although the difference was not statistically significant between quintiles of the conditional distribution.
In the same study, actual drinking levels in drinking families were not at all or only weakly associated with offspring drinking 10 years later, and supplementary analyses confirmed these patterns.
The study authors note that the relationship between parental and offspring drinking appears more complex than often assumed and has rarely been tracked over long periods.

Other supplied studies concern adolescent alcohol use (parental support, school context, puberty), prenatal alcohol exposure and child ADHD symptoms, or suicidal behavior and substance use liability; they do not assess familial drinking transmission into young adulthood.

uncertainty: Evidence is essentially from a single Swedish cohort, so generalizability is unclear. Persistence appears limited to an abstainer versus non-abstainer distinction rather than a graded dose-response relationship, and the evidence does not establish mechanisms (genetic versus environmental). The remaining records are indirect and cannot confirm or refute persistence.

question: Does the treatment of amblyopia normalise subfoveal choroidal thickness in amblyopic children?
answer: The one relevant study (PMID:27757987) found that six months of amblyopia treatment improved visual acuity but did not significantly change subfoveal choroidal thickness, and amblyopic eyes remained thicker than fellow eyes after treatment. Treatment therefore did not normalise choroidal thickness in that sample.

claims.text: In 32 anisometropic hyperopic children with unilateral amblyopia, treatment (full refractive correction, adaptation phase, and patching of the fellow eye) improved amblyopic-eye visual acuity from 0.35 ± 0.3 to 0.16 ± 0.2 logMAR (p < 0.001).
Before treatment, mean choroidal thickness was significantly higher in amblyopic eyes than in fellow eyes (p = 0.019).
There were no significant pre- versus post-treatment differences in mean choroidal thickness in amblyopic eyes (p = 0.428) or fellow eyes (p = 0.343).
After treatment, choroidal thickness remained higher in amblyopic eyes than in fellow eyes (p = 0.006), so it was not normalised.

uncertainty: The conclusion rests on a single small prospective study (n=32) of anisometropic hyperopic unilateral amblyopia with six months of follow-up. Results may not generalise to other amblyopia types (e.g., strabismic), longer treatment durations, or other populations. The study had no untreated control group, and the other evidence records do not address choroidal thickness after treatment.

question: Prostate bed target interfractional motion using RTOG consensus definitions and daily CT on rails : Does target motion differ between superior and inferior portions of the clinical target volume?
answer: In the one directly relevant study (8 patients, 300 fractions), prostate bed target motion did not differ significantly between the superior and inferior portions of the CTV in any direction.

claims.text: The study defined INF-CTV and SUP-CTV as the PB-CTV inferior and superior to the superior border of the pubic symphysis, and compared daily CT-on-rails images to the planning CT in LR, SI, and AP directions in 8 postprostatectomy patients (300 fractions).
Mean INF-CTV target motion was 0.1 (±2.8), 0.5 (±2.2), and 0.2 (±2.5) mm in LR, SI, and AP directions, and mean SUP-CTV target motion was 0.3 (±1.8), 0.5 (±2.3), and 0 (±5.0) mm.
No statistically significant differences between INF-CTV and SUP-CTV motion were found in any direction.
Overall PB-CTV target motion (bone to RTOG-defined anatomy) had small means (0.2, 0.3, 0 mm in LR, SI, AP), whereas total motion from skin tattoos was larger (-1.5, 1.3, 3.7 mm).
The SUP-CTV AP motion showed a numerically larger variability (SD 5.0 mm) than INF-CTV AP (SD 2.5 mm), though this was not statistically significant.

uncertainty: Evidence comes from a single small study of 8 patients, so it may lack power to detect real differences, particularly the larger SD in SUP-CTV AP motion. Other supplied records address different topics and do not inform this question.

question: Do prerecorded lecture VODcasts affect lecture attendance of first-yearpre-clinical Graduate Entry to Medicine students?
answer: The one directly relevant study (PMID:28027677) found that attendance stayed high when prerecorded Physiology VODcasts were available to first-year GEM students, suggesting no meaningful reduction in live lecture attendance. This rests on self-reported survey data without a control group.

claims.text: In surveys of first-year GEM students where prerecorded Physiology VODcasts were available before live lectures, 84.3% of respondents attended all 21 lectures.
Only 4% of students missed more than one lecture in each of the three lecture series.
79% of students indicated that VODcasts should not replace live lectures.
The survey response rate was 191/214 (89%).

The other evidence records address patient-safety curricula, remote OSCE examiners, online masters programmes, and teacher training, and do not address the effect of VODcasts on attendance in this population.

uncertainty: The evidence comes from a single study using surveys, so attendance was likely self-reported. There was no comparison group without VODcasts, so a causal effect cannot be established. It covered Physiology lectures at one institution and may not generalize to other subjects or settings. The abstract excerpt does not give a baseline attendance rate.

question: Are serum leptin levels a prognostic factor in advanced lung cancer?
answer: The only evidence directly testing leptin as a prognostic marker found no association between serum leptin and overall survival in lung cancer patients. The other records do not address leptin and prognosis, so the evidence is limited to one small study.

claims.text: In 71 previously untreated lung cancer patients, serum leptin analysis did not show any association with overall survival.

Serum leptin at diagnosis was significantly lower in lung cancer patients than in matched controls (4.75±4.91 vs 9.67±8.02 ng/ml; p<0.001), and it did not differ by ECOG PS, weight loss, histological type, disease stage or TNM classification.
A separate case-control study found elevated serum leptin was associated with NSCLC risk (OR 4.58), but this concerns disease risk and not prognosis or survival.
Established prognostic factors in advanced NSCLC in one cohort were absence of weight loss, cytostatic treatment and ECOG 0-1; leptin was not among the variables analyzed.

uncertainty: Evidence on leptin and survival comes from a single small study (n=71) that did not restrict to advanced disease, so a modest prognostic effect cannot be excluded. The study also reported an inconsistent correlation statistic (p>0.010) for leptin and BMI. The other records (obesity NADPH oxidase, IL-6 and recurrence) do not address serum leptin prognosis in lung cancer. This is research summarization, not medical advice.
